Topic 03·Anik Sir · Lectures 3–4

LTI systems and convolution

Linearity, time invariance, the impulse response, and convolution sums and integrals.

4 past questions on this topic

Systems: signals in, signals out

A system transforms an input signal into an output signal. We write x(t)→y(t)x(t)\to y(t)x(t)→y(t) or x[n]→y[n]x[n]\to y[n]x[n]→y[n].

An ordinary function takes one number and returns one number. A system takes a whole signal (a whole function) and returns another whole signal. A filter, an amplifier, an echo chamber and a camera sensor are all systems.

Two properties that make life easy

Linearity

A system is linear if it obeys two rules:

  1. Homogeneity (scaling): if x(t)→y(t)x(t)\to y(t)x(t)→y(t), then a x(t)→a y(t)a\,x(t)\to a\,y(t)ax(t)→ay(t).
  2. Additivity: if x1→y1x_1\to y_1x1​→y1​ and x2→y2x_2\to y_2x2​→y2​, then x1+x2→y1+y2x_1+x_2\to y_1+y_2x1​+x2​→y1​+y2​.

Together they form superposition: a x1+b x2→a y1+b y2a\,x_1+b\,x_2\to a\,y_1+b\,y_2ax1​+bx2​→ay1​+by2​. You can treat the pieces of an input separately and add the outputs.

Consequences and quick tests:

  • Put a=0a=0a=0: zero input must give zero output. y=x+1y=x+1y=x+1 fails this, so it is not linear.
  • y=3x(t)y=3x(t)y=3x(t), y=dxdty=\frac{dx}{dt}y=dtdx​, y=∫x dty=\int x\,dty=∫xdt are linear; y=x2(t)y=x^2(t)y=x2(t) is not (doubling xxx quadruples yyy).

Time invariance

A system is time invariant if delaying the input only delays the output:

x(t)→y(t)⟹x(t−t0)→y(t−t0)  for every t0.x(t)\to y(t)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x(t-t_0)\to y(t-t_0)\ \text{ for every } t_0 .x(t)→y(t)⟹x(t−t0​)→y(t−t0​)  for every t0​.

How to test: (1) feed the shifted input x(t−t0)x(t-t_0)x(t−t0​) and compute the output; (2) shift the original output to get y(t−t0)y(t-t_0)y(t−t0​); (3) compare.

  • y(t)=x(t−1)y(t)=x(t-1)y(t)=x(t−1) and y(t)=x2(t)y(t)=x^2(t)y(t)=x2(t) are time invariant.
  • y(t)=t x(t)y(t)=t\,x(t)y(t)=tx(t) is not: feeding x(t−t0)x(t-t_0)x(t−t0​) gives t x(t−t0)t\,x(t-t_0)tx(t−t0​), but y(t−t0)=(t−t0) x(t−t0)y(t-t_0)=(t-t_0)\,x(t-t_0)y(t−t0​)=(t−t0​)x(t−t0​).
  • y(t)=x(2t)y(t)=x(2t)y(t)=x(2t) is not: feeding x(t−t0)x(t-t_0)x(t−t0​) gives x(2t−t0)x(2t-t_0)x(2t−t0​), but y(t−t0)=x(2t−2t0)y(t-t_0)=x(2t-2t_0)y(t−t0​)=x(2t−2t0​).

LTI systems

A system that is both linear and time invariant is called LTI. Why we care: for an LTI system, the response to one special input lets us compute the output for any input. That special input is the impulse, and the tool is convolution.

A detour: convolution as polynomial multiplication

Convolution is just another way of combining two sequences, like adding or subtracting them, but it mixes them differently. It appears naturally when you multiply polynomials.

A(z)=1+3z+2z2+5z3+4z4,B(z)=2−z+4z2+z3+3z4.A(z)=1+3z+2z^2+5z^3+4z^4,\qquad B(z)=2-z+4z^2+z^3+3z^4 .A(z)=1+3z+2z2+5z3+4z4,B(z)=2−z+4z2+z3+3z4.

What is the coefficient of z4z^4z4 in A(z)B(z)A(z)B(z)A(z)B(z)? Collect every product whose powers add to 4: a0b4, a1b3, a2b2, a3b1, a4b0a_0b_4,\ a_1b_3,\ a_2b_2,\ a_3b_1,\ a_4b_0a0​b4​, a1​b3​, a2​b2​, a3​b1​, a4​b0​.

c[4]=1⋅3+3⋅1+2⋅4+5⋅(−1)+4⋅2=17.\begin{aligned}&c[4]\\[6pt]&= 1\cdot3+3\cdot1+2\cdot4+5\cdot(-1)+4\cdot2\\[6pt]&= 17 .\end{aligned}​c[4]=1⋅3+3⋅1+2⋅4+5⋅(−1)+4⋅2=17.​

In general, the coefficient of znz^nzn pairs up indices that add to nnn:

c[n]=∑ka[k] b[n−k].c[n]=\sum_k a[k]\,b[n-k].c[n]=k∑​a[k]b[n−k].

Reflection turns crossed pairs into vertical pairs

The index b[n−k]b[n-k]b[n−k] means: reflect bbb (so b[k]→b[−k]b[k]\to b[-k]b[k]→b[−k]), then shift it right by nnn. Now the pairs that multiply sit directly above each other.

  • n=0n=0n=0: only a[0]b[0]=1⋅2=2a[0]b[0]=1\cdot2=2a[0]b[0]=1⋅2=2 overlaps, so c[0]=2c[0]=2c[0]=2.
  • n=2n=2n=2: c[2]=1⋅4+3⋅(−1)+2⋅2=5c[2]=1\cdot4+3\cdot(-1)+2\cdot2=5c[2]=1⋅4+3⋅(−1)+2⋅2=5.
  • n=4n=4n=4: all five pairs line up, giving the same c[4]=17c[4]=17c[4]=17 as before.

Convolution: keep the first signal as it is, reflect the second, slide it right to position nnn, multiply the overlapping samples and add. One position gives one output value.

c[n]=(a∗b)[n]=∑k=−∞∞a[k] b[n−k]\begin{aligned}&c[n]\\[6pt]&= (a*b)[n]\\[6pt]&= \sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}a[k]\,b[n-k]\end{aligned}​c[n]=(a∗b)[n]=k=−∞∑∞​a[k]b[n−k]​

Order does not matter. Since A(z)B(z)=B(z)A(z)A(z)B(z)=B(z)A(z)A(z)B(z)=B(z)A(z), convolution is commutative: a∗b=b∗aa*b=b*aa∗b=b∗a. You may reflect whichever signal is easier.

Why convolution matters

Goal: find the output of an LTI system for any input. The philosophy is the same as counting the factors of 72=23⋅3272=2^3\cdot3^272=23⋅32: solve the easy pieces (20..232^0..2^320..23 gives 4 choices, 30..323^0..3^230..32 gives 3), then combine them (4⋅3=124\cdot3=124⋅3=12 factors). For systems:

  1. Solve for the simplest input.
  2. Break any input into simple pieces.
  3. Combine the small answers.

Step 1: the impulse response

The simplest input is the impulse δ[n]\delta[n]δ[n]: zero everywhere except one instant. The output it produces is the impulse response:

δ[n] ⟶ h[n].\delta[n]\ \longrightarrow\ h[n].δ[n] ⟶ h[n].

Like poking a sleeping cat and watching how it reacts, the impulse response is the system's signature.

  • Echo system. One short "hello" produces equal echoes forever: h[n]=u[n]h[n]=u[n]h[n]=u[n].
  • Fading echoes. h[n]=αnu[n]h[n]=\alpha^nu[n]h[n]=αnu[n] with 0<α<10<\alpha<10<α<1: each echo keeps a fraction α\alphaα of the previous one. Large α\alphaα means slow fading; small α\alphaα means the echoes die quickly.
  • Pure delay. y[n]=x[n−3]y[n]=x[n-3]y[n]=x[n−3] has h[n]=δ[n−3]h[n]=\delta[n-3]h[n]=δ[n−3] (and h(t)=δ(t−3)h(t)=\delta(t-3)h(t)=δ(t−3) in continuous time).

Step 2 and 3: one example by hand

Send x[n]=δ[n]+2δ[n−1]−δ[n−2]+δ[n−3]x[n]=\delta[n]+2\delta[n-1]-\delta[n-2]+\delta[n-3]x[n]=δ[n]+2δ[n−1]−δ[n−2]+δ[n−3] into the echo system h[n]=u[n]h[n]=u[n]h[n]=u[n].

By the two LTI properties:

  • time invariance: δ[n−k]→h[n−k]=u[n−k]\delta[n-k]\to h[n-k]=u[n-k]δ[n−k]→h[n−k]=u[n−k];
  • homogeneity: a δ[n−k]→a u[n−k]a\,\delta[n-k]\to a\,u[n-k]aδ[n−k]→au[n−k];
  • additivity: add the four outputs.
y[n]=u[n]+2u[n−1]−u[n−2]+u[n−3],y[n]=u[n]+2u[n-1]-u[n-2]+u[n-3],y[n]=u[n]+2u[n−1]−u[n−2]+u[n−3],

which is {1,3,2,3,3,3,… }\{1,3,2,3,3,3,\dots\}{1,3,2,3,3,3,…} starting at n=0n=0n=0.

The general case: the convolution sum

Any discrete input is a stack of scaled, shifted impulses (the sifting identity from the previous topic):

x[n]=∑k=−∞∞x[k] δ[n−k].x[n]=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}x[k]\,\delta[n-k].x[n]=k=−∞∑∞​x[k]δ[n−k].

The value x[k]x[k]x[k] is the height of the impulse placed at n=kn=kn=k. Each piece produces a piece of output:

x[k] δ[n−k] → TI + homogeneity  x[k] h[n−k],x[k]\,\delta[n-k]\ \xrightarrow{\ \text{TI + homogeneity}\ }\ x[k]\,h[n-k],x[k]δ[n−k]  TI + homogeneity ​ x[k]h[n−k],

and additivity adds them all:

 y[n]=∑k=−∞∞x[k] h[n−k]=(x∗h)[n] \boxed{\,y[n]=\sum_{k=-\infty}^{\infty}x[k]\,h[n-k]=(x*h)[n]\,}y[n]=k=−∞∑∞​x[k]h[n−k]=(x∗h)[n]​

The bridge is complete. (1) Find hhh, the response to δ\deltaδ. (2) Break the input into shifted impulses. (3) Shift, scale and add copies of hhh. That sum is convolution.

Continuous-time convolution

The same idea with an integral instead of a sum:

 y(t)=(x∗h)(t)=∫−∞∞x(τ) h(t−τ) dτ \boxed{\,y(t)=(x*h)(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)\,h(t-\tau)\,d\tau\,}y(t)=(x∗h)(t)=∫−∞∞​x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ​

For a fixed ttt, reflect h(τ)→h(−τ)h(\tau)\to h(-\tau)h(τ)→h(−τ), shift it to h(t−τ)h(t-\tau)h(t−τ), multiply by x(τ)x(\tau)x(τ) and integrate over the overlap. As ttt changes, h(t−τ)h(t-\tau)h(t−τ) slides along the τ\tauτ axis.

The recipe, both domains:

  1. Choose the output location (nnn or ttt).
  2. Reflect and shift the second signal: h[k]→h[−k]→h[n−k]h[k]\to h[-k]\to h[n-k]h[k]→h[−k]→h[n−k], or h(τ)→h(−τ)→h(t−τ)h(\tau)\to h(-\tau)\to h(t-\tau)h(τ)→h(−τ)→h(t−τ).
  3. Multiply where they overlap, then add (sum over kkk) or integrate (over τ\tauτ).
  4. The overlap region changes at "break points"; treat each range of nnn or ttt as a separate case.

Properties of convolution

propertystatementwhat it means for systems

Exam pointers

  • Always draw (or describe) h[n−k]h[n-k]h[n−k] as a function of kkk and mark where its edge sits. Then list the cases of nnn where the overlap changes.
  • Two-sided inputs: split with the distributive property and convolve each side.
  • Shifted steps such as (14)nu[n+3]\left(\frac14\right)^nu[n+3](41​)nu[n+3]: rewrite as 64(14)n+3u[n+3]64\left(\frac14\right)^{n+3}u[n+3]64(41​)n+3u[n+3], convolve with the unshifted signal, then shift the result by time invariance.
  • "Prove y=x∗hy=x*hy=x∗h using only time-domain analysis": sifting + time invariance + homogeneity + additivity, in that order.
  • Check one output value by direct summation before finishing.
